claim: Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) maintains epigenetic repression of many genes in animals and plants.
source: The conserved Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) maintains epigenetic repression of many genes in animals and plants and modifies chromatin at its targets.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PRC2 function in the abstract.

claim: PRC2 modifies chromatin at its targets.
source: The conserved Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) maintains epigenetic repression of many genes in animals and plants and modifies chromatin at its targets.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PRC2 function in the abstract.

claim: Histones modified by PRC2 can be inherited through cell division.
source: Histones modified by PRC2 can be inherited through cell division.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: One copy of FLC can be repressed while the other is active in the same plants.
source: By monitoring the expression of two copies of the Arabidopsis Polycomb target gene FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) in the same plants, we show that one copy can be repressed while the other is active.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: The 'mixed' expression state of FLC is inherited through many cell divisions as plants develop.
source: Furthermore, this 'mixed' expression state is inherited through many cell divisions as plants develop.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Epigenetic memory of FLC expression is stored in cis, not in trans.
source: These data demonstrate that epigenetic memory of FLC expression is stored not in trans but in cis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Trans memory involves storage of epigenetic memory in the concentrations of diffusible regulatory factors that are maintained through feedback loops.
source: Epigenetic memory can be stored in the concentrations of diffusible regulatory factors that are maintained through feedback loops (trans memory) (Novick and Weiner, 1957; Ptashne, 2004; Zacharioudakis et al., 2007 ; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cis memory involves storage of epigenetic memory locally in the chromatin environment of individual genes in the form of DNA methylation or post-translational modifications of histones.
source: Alternatively, memory could be stored locally in the chromatin environment of individual genes (cis memory), in the form of DNA methylation or post-translational modifications of histones (Moazed, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In trans memory, chromatin responds to the transcriptional state defined by heritable concentrations of trans-factors.
source: While in both trans and cis memory the chromatin state is inherited, in the former case chromatin responds to the transcriptional state defined by heritable concentrations of the trans-factors, whereas in the latter case it is the local chromatin environment that instructs its own inheritance and is, therefore, the key epigenetic memory element.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction explained in the introduction.

claim: In cis memory, the local chromatin environment instructs its own inheritance and is the key epigenetic memory element.
source: While in both trans and cis memory the chromatin state is inherited, in the former case chromatin responds to the transcriptional state defined by heritable concentrations of the trans-factors, whereas in the latter case it is the local chromatin environment that instructs its own inheritance and is, therefore, the key epigenetic memory element.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction explained in the introduction.

claim: PRC2 catalyses methylation of histone H3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me).
source: PRC2 catalyses methylation of histone H3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me) (Cao et al., 2002) and mutagenesis experiments have shown that K27 is necessary for PRC2-mediated repression (Pengelly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: K27 is necessary for PRC2-mediated repression.
source: PRC2 catalyses methylation of histone H3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me) (Cao et al., 2002) and mutagenesis experiments have shown that K27 is necessary for PRC2-mediated repression (Pengelly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: During replication, maternal histones are shared between daughter chromosomes where they re-associate close to their original location.
source: During replication, maternal histones are shared between daughter chromosomes where they re-associate close to their original location (Radman-Livaja et al., 2011; Annunziato, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PRC2 has affinity for H3K27me3.
source: Since PRC2 has affinity for H3K27me3, it has been proposed that H3K27me3 on inherited histones could recruit PRC2 to daughter DNA strands in order to similarly modify newly incorporated, unmodified histones (Margueron et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: H3K27me3 on inherited histones could recruit PRC2 to daughter DNA strands to modify newly incorporated, unmodified histones.
source: Since PRC2 has affinity for H3K27me3, it has been proposed that H3K27me3 on inherited histones could recruit PRC2 to daughter DNA strands in order to similarly modify newly incorporated, unmodified histones (Margueron et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work cited in the introduction.

claim: Passage of H3K27-methylated histones to daughter chromosomes can occur in the absence of functional PRC2.
source: Supporting the hypothesis that modified histones are indeed the key inherited cis memory element, it was recently observed that passage of H3K27-methylated histones to daughter chromosomes can occur in the absence of functional PRC2 (Gaydos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Polycomb proteins themselves are maintained locally through DNA replication.
source: Other studies have suggested that Polycomb proteins themselves are maintained locally through DNA replication (Petruk et al., 2012; Francis et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: To definitively demonstrate that memory is stored in cis, it is necessary to show that two copies of the same DNA sequence can be independently maintained in different transcriptional states in the same nucleus.
source: However, to definitively demonstrate that memory is stored in cis, it is necessary to show that two copies of the same DNA sequence can be independently maintained in different transcriptional states in the same nucleus (Bonasio et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a criterion for demonstrating cis memory, supported by a citation.

claim: Cis memory has been observed in genomic imprinting.
source: This has been observed in genomic imprinting and in random X-chromosome inactivation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Cis memory has been observed in random X-chromosome inactivation.
source: This has been observed in genomic imprinting and in random X-chromosome inactivation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Genomic imprinting involves DNA methylation.
source: Since imprinting involves DNA methylation (Ferguson-Smith, 2011), and X-chromosome inactivation involves chromosome-wide changes in chromatin structure and nuclear positioning (Gendrel et al., 2014), it remains an open question whether Polycomb-repressed chromatin at a single gene can store epigenetic memory.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: X-chromosome inactivation involves chromosome-wide changes in chromatin structure and nuclear positioning.
source: Since imprinting involves DNA methylation (Ferguson-Smith, 2011), and X-chromosome inactivation involves chromosome-wide changes in chromatin structure and nuclear positioning (Gendrel et al., 2014), it remains an open question whether Polycomb-repressed chromatin at a single gene can store epigenetic memory.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Vernalization is the acceleration of flowering following prolonged cold exposure.
source: Vernalization is the acceleration of flowering following prolonged cold exposure and is mediated by cold-induced epigenetic repression of the Polycomb target gene and floral repressor FLC.
evidence: This is a definition of vernalization stated in the introduction.

claim: Vernalization is mediated by cold-induced epigenetic repression of FLC.
source: Vernalization is the acceleration of flowering following prolonged cold exposure and is mediated by cold-induced epigenetic repression of the Polycomb target gene and floral repressor FLC.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: FLC repression requires PRC2.
source: FLC repression requires PRC2 but is independent of DNA methylation (Finnegan et al., 2005), making it a useful system for studying the cis-memory storage capability of Polycomb at a single gene.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: FLC repression is independent of DNA methylation.
source: FLC repression requires PRC2 but is independent of DNA methylation (Finnegan et al., 2005), making it a useful system for studying the cis-memory storage capability of Polycomb at a single gene.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In vernalized plants, FLC expression is bistable.
source: In vernalized plants, FLC expression is bistable, with the number of cells in which FLC is stably repressed increasing quantitatively with the duration of prior cold exposure (Angel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The number of cells in which FLC is stably repressed increases quantitatively with the duration of prior cold exposure.
source: In vernalized plants, FLC expression is bistable, with the number of cells in which FLC is stably repressed increasing quantitatively with the duration of prior cold exposure (Angel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cold exposure results in localization of a plant-homeodomain-PRC2 complex (PHD-PRC2) to a small nucleation region within the FLC gene.
source: Cold exposure results in localization of a plant-homeodomain-PRC2 complex (PHD-PRC2) to a small nucleation region within the FLC gene, which leads to locally increased H3K27me3 and co-ordinately decreased H3K36me3 (Angel et al., 2011; De Lucia et al., 2008; Finnegan and Dennis, 2007; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PHD-PRC2 localization leads to locally increased H3K27me3 and co-ordinately decreased H3K36me3.
source: Cold exposure results in localization of a plant-homeodomain-PRC2 complex (PHD-PRC2) to a small nucleation region within the FLC gene, which leads to locally increased H3K27me3 and co-ordinately decreased H3K36me3 (Angel et al., 2011; De Lucia et al., 2008; Finnegan and Dennis, 2007; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: On return to warm, the PHD-PRC2 complex spreads across the FLC gene leading to high H3K27me3 over the whole locus and stable repression.
source: On return to warm, the PHD-PRC2 complex spreads across the gene leading to high H3K27me3 over the whole locus and stable repression (Angel et al., 2011; De Lucia et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: After cold, H3K27me3 is present at the FLC promoter and gene body but does not spread to neighbouring genes.
source: After cold, H3K27me3 is present at the FLC promoter and gene body but does not spread to neighbouring genes (Angel et al., 2011; Finnegan and Dennis, 2007; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Polycomb-dependent FLC repression is maintained throughout plant development until it is reset during embryogenesis.
source: Polycomb-dependent FLC repression is maintained throughout plant development until it is reset during embryogenesis (Gendall et al., 2001; Crevillen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: If FLC transcriptional states are defined by concentrations of diffusible factors (trans memory), then all copies of FLC within a cell should be in the same transcriptional state.
source: If FLC transcriptional states are defined by concentrations of diffusible factors (trans memory), then all copies of FLC within a cell should be in the same transcriptional state.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the definition of trans memory.

claim: If FLC chromatin states instruct their own inheritance (cis memory), then it should be possible for different copies of FLC within a cell to exist in different heritable transcriptional states.
source: On the other hand, if FLC chromatin states instruct their own inheritance (cis memory), then it should be possible for different copies of FLC within a cell to exist in different heritable transcriptional states.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the definition of cis memory.

claim: The transgenes consist of 12 kb of genomic DNA surrounding FLC with the Venus or mCherry sequence inserted as a translational fusion into FLC exon 6.
source: The transgenes consist of 12 kb of genomic DNA surrounding FLC with the Venus or mCherry sequence inserted as a translational fusion into FLC exon 6 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental construct and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The early flowering phenotype of flc-2 mutants was fully rescued in transgenic lines.
source: The early flowering phenotype of flc-2 mutants was fully rescued in transgenic lines, demonstrating that the fusion proteins are functional (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The FLC-Venus and FLC-mCherry fusion proteins are functional.
source: The early flowering phenotype of flc-2 mutants was fully rescued in transgenic lines, demonstrating that the fusion proteins are functional (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of the flc-2 phenotype.

claim: Expression of full-length FLC-Venus fusion protein was confirmed by immunoprecipitation, followed by immunoblot and mass spectrometry.
source: Expression of full-length FLC-Venus fusion protein was confirmed by immunoprecipitation, followed by immunoblot and mass spectrometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: FLC-Venus and FLC-mCherry plants responded to cold exposure by accelerating flowering.
source: Like wild-type Columbia line FRI-sf2 (Col-FRI), FLC-Venus and FLC-mCherry plants responded to cold exposure by accelerating flowering (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The FLC transgenes were stably repressed similarly to endogenous FLC after cold.
source: This indicates that the FLC transgenes were stably repressed similarly to endogenous FLC after cold.
evidence: This is inferred from the flowering time data.

claim: Epigenetic repression of FLC-Venus was quantitatively dependent on the duration of cold exposure at the transcriptional level in both roots and shoots.
source: Epigenetic repression was confirmed to be quantitatively dependent on the duration of cold exposure for FLC-Venus at the transcriptional level in both roots and shoots, and also at the protein level (Figure 2A, Figure 2–figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2–figure supplement 1.

claim: Epigenetic repression of FLC-Venus was quantitatively dependent on the duration of cold exposure at the protein level.
source: Epigenetic repression was confirmed to be quantitatively dependent on the duration of cold exposure for FLC-Venus at the transcriptional level in both roots and shoots, and also at the protein level (Figure 2A, Figure 2–figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2–figure supplement 1.

claim: The FLC antisense transcripts, named COOLAIR, are expressed from these constructs.
source: We also verified that the FLC antisense transcripts, named COOLAIR (Swiezewski et al., 2009; Csorba et al., 2014), are expressed from these constructs and are induced during cold exposure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: COOLAIR transcripts are induced during cold exposure.
source: We also verified that the FLC antisense transcripts, named COOLAIR (Swiezewski et al., 2009; Csorba et al., 2014), are expressed from these constructs and are induced during cold exposure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Roots provide an excellent system for studying heritability of epigenetic states because cell lineages are visible as continuous files of cells that arise from repeated anticlinal divisions along the longitudinal axis of the growing root.
source: Roots provide an excellent system for studying heritability of epigenetic states because cell lineages are visible as continuous files of cells that arise from repeated anticlinal divisions along the longitudinal axis of the growing root (Dolan et al., 1993) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: In warm conditions, stem cells at the root tip divide approximately once every two days.
source: In warm conditions, stem cells at the root tip divide approximately once every two days, while for other meristematic cells this occurs approximately once per day (Campilho et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: For other meristematic cells, cell division occurs approximately once per day in warm conditions.
source: In warm conditions, stem cells at the root tip divide approximately once every two days, while for other meristematic cells this occurs approximately once per day (Campilho et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 7 days after plants are transferred from cold, a single cell in the stem cell niche will have given rise to a lineage that encompasses a long file of cells in the root meristem.
source: Therefore, 7 days after plants are transferred from cold, a single cell in the stem cell niche will have given rise to a lineage that encompasses a long file of cells in the root meristem.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell division rates.

claim: Images of FLC-Venus and FLC-mCherry 7 days after cold exposure showed long files of cells in the same expression state.
source: Strikingly, images of FLC-Venus and FLC-mCherry 7 days after cold exposure showed long files of cells in the same expression state (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), demonstrating the long-term mitotic stability of the active and repressed transcriptional states.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in multiple figures.

claim: Long files of cells in the same expression state demonstrate the long-term mitotic stability of the active and repressed transcriptional states.
source: Strikingly, images of FLC-Venus and FLC-mCherry 7 days after cold exposure showed long files of cells in the same expression state (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), demonstrating the long-term mitotic stability of the active and repressed transcriptional states.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of long files of cells in the same state.

claim: The number of cells expressing FLC-Venus decreased quantitatively with the duration of cold exposure.
source: As suggested by individual images, our unbiased analysis of 53 roots (8547 reconstructed cells) revealed that the number of cells expressing FLC-Venus decreased quantitatively with the duration of cold exposure (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is an experimental result from quantitative image analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: FLC-Venus expression was bimodal after 6 or 8 weeks cold.
source: Importantly, FLC-Venus expression was bimodal after 6 or 8 weeks cold, and almost all cells were silenced after 10 weeks cold (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Almost all cells were silenced after 10 weeks cold.
source: Importantly, FLC-Venus expression was bimodal after 6 or 8 weeks cold, and almost all cells were silenced after 10 weeks cold (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Non-vernalized roots showed uniform ON/ON expression of both transgenes in all cells.
source: As expected, non-vernalized roots showed uniform ON/ON expression of both transgenes in all cells (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Long files of cells were observed in which one FLC reporter was stably repressed, while the other remained stably activated.
source: Strikingly, we observed long files of cells in which one FLC reporter was stably repressed, while the other remained stably activated (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a key experimental observation shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Long-term mitotic stability of all four possible combinations was observed: FLC-Venus/FLC-mCherry ON/ON, ON/OFF, OFF/ON, and OFF/OFF.
source: In fact, we observed long-term mitotic stability of all four possible combinations: FLC-Venus/FLC-mCherry ON/ON, ON/OFF, OFF/ON, and OFF/OFF (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a key experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inheritance of the 'mixed' ON/OFF and OFF/ON states directly contradicts trans memory.
source: Inheritance of the 'mixed' ON/OFF and OFF/ON states directly contradicts trans memory and instead provides direct evidence of a cis-encoded epigenetic state at FLC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Inheritance of the 'mixed' ON/OFF and OFF/ON states provides direct evidence of a cis-encoded epigenetic state at FLC.
source: Inheritance of the 'mixed' ON/OFF and OFF/ON states directly contradicts trans memory and instead provides direct evidence of a cis-encoded epigenetic state at FLC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The FLC-Venus and FLC-mCherry transgenes in double-hemizygous F1 plants are not in the same genomic location.
source: The FLC-Venus and FLC-mCherry transgenes in these double-hemizygous F1 plants are not in the same genomic location.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the experimental system.

claim: The reporters are actively expressed throughout development in warm conditions and epigenetically repressed specifically in response to prolonged cold.
source: However, like endogenous FLC, the reporters are actively expressed throughout development in warm conditions and epigenetically repressed specifically in response to prolonged cold (Figures 1–3, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in multiple figures.

claim: Epigenetic repression depends on cold exposure and the FLC-specific sequences within the transgenes rather than the genomic location.
source: Epigenetic repression, therefore, depends on cold exposure and the FLC-specific sequences within the transgenes rather than the genomic location.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both transgenes respond to cold despite being in different locations.

claim: Similar numbers of cells are observed in the FLC-Venus/FLC-mCherry ON/OFF and OFF/ON expression states.
source: Furthermore, since we observe similar numbers of cells in the FLC-Venus/FLC-mCherry ON/OFF and OFF/ON expression states (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we consider it unlikely that differences in genomic location or fluorophore sequence between the transgenes causes one of the copies to be preferentially repressed over the other.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Differences in genomic location or fluorophore sequence between the transgenes are unlikely to cause one of the copies to be preferentially repressed over the other.
source: Furthermore, since we observe similar numbers of cells in the FLC-Venus/FLC-mCherry ON/OFF and OFF/ON expression states (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we consider it unlikely that differences in genomic location or fluorophore sequence between the transgenes causes one of the copies to be preferentially repressed over the other.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar numbers of ON/OFF and OFF/ON cells.

claim: The molecular changes to the chromatin environment of FLC induced by prolonged cold exposure are sufficient to instruct epigenetic inheritance of the Polycomb-repressed transcriptional state.
source: Our findings demonstrate that the molecular changes to the chromatin environment of FLC induced by prolonged cold exposure are sufficient to instruct epigenetic inheritance of the Polycomb-repressed transcriptional state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Polycomb complex binding and H3K27me may not be the only factors that constitute the locally encoded epigenetic state.
source: However, Polycomb complex binding and H3K27me may not be the only factors that constitute this locally encoded epigenetic state.
evidence: This is speculation about additional factors that may be involved.

claim: Specific nucleic acid structures may play important roles in the locally encoded epigenetic state.
source: Specific nucleic acid structures (Klose et al., 2013), non-coding RNAs (Herzog et al., 2014) (for example the chromatin-associated COOLAIR antisense transcripts at FLC (Csorba et al., 2014)), and histone variants (Jacob et al., 2014) may also play important roles.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Non-coding RNAs may play important roles in the locally encoded epigenetic state.
source: Specific nucleic acid structures (Klose et al., 2013), non-coding RNAs (Herzog et al., 2014) (for example the chromatin-associated COOLAIR antisense transcripts at FLC (Csorba et al., 2014)), and histone variants (Jacob et al., 2014) may also play important roles.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Histone variants may play important roles in the locally encoded epigenetic state.
source: Specific nucleic acid structures (Klose et al., 2013), non-coding RNAs (Herzog et al., 2014) (for example the chromatin-associated COOLAIR antisense transcripts at FLC (Csorba et al., 2014)), and histone variants (Jacob et al., 2014) may also play important roles.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Not all H3K27-methylated chromatin should be considered as epigenetically silent.
source: Thus, not all H3K27-methylated chromatin should be considered as epigenetically silent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discussion.

claim: The predicted mass of FLC-Venus is 48.8 kDa.
source: The predicted mass of FLC-Venus is 48.8 kDa.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Repeated anticlinal cell divisions give rise to clonal cell files along the axis of growth in Arabidopsis root meristems.
source: Schematic of an Arabidopsis root meristem showing how repeated anticlinal cell divisions give rise to clonal cell files along the axis of growth.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 2B and is established knowledge.

claim: FLC-Venus is localized to nuclei.
source: FLC-Venus is localized to nuclei.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 2C.

claim: In a trans memory system, only two mitotically heritable states are possible (FLC-Venus/FLC-mCherry ON/ON, OFF/OFF).
source: In a trans memory system, the two copies of FLC are coordinately regulated and only two mitotically heritable states are possible (FLC-Venus/FLC-mCherry ON/ON, OFF/OFF).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the definition of trans memory, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: In a cis memory system, four mitotically heritable states are possible (FLC-Venus/FLC-mCherry ON/ON, ON/OFF, OFF/ON, OFF/OFF).
source: In a cis memory system, the two copies of FLC can be maintained in alternative expression states, so four mitotically heritable states are possible (FLC-Venus/FLC-mCherry ON/ON, ON/OFF, OFF/ON, OFF/OFF).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the definition of cis memory, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The transgenes extend from 3.4 kb upstream to 8.6 kb downstream of the FLC transcription start site.
source: Transgenes extend from 3.4 kb upstream to 8.6 kb downstream of the FLC transcription start site.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A.

claim: Vernalized plants were pre-grown for 1 week at 22°C and spent 4 weeks at 5°C before being returned to 22°C.
source: Vernalized plants were pre-grown for 1 week at 22°C and spent 4 weeks at 5°C before being returned to 22°C.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C.

claim: Flowering time is counted in days from sowing until bolting but does not include time spent in cold.
source: Flowering time is counted in days from sowing until bolting but does not include time spent in cold.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C.
